whyDsl.title: Why?
whyDsl.description: SQL has been the foundation of data work for decades. It's powerful, expressive, and universal. But for some tasks, it can get in the way.
bullets: SQL blurs the lines between <1>what</1> you want and <3>how</3> to get it.
Results don't help you discover relationships or context in your schema.
SQL wasn't designed with visual exploration in mind.
whyDsl.closing: SQL is great - but we can improve the experience with a domain-specific language (DSL).

pineLang.title: Introducing Pine-lang
pineLang.description: Beamlynx uses pine-lang which is an intuitive query language that transpiles to SQL. Pine-lang uses a pipe-based syntax inspired by Unix pipes, making queries readable and composable. As you write queries, you see a real-time visualization of table relationships.

table.title: Table
table.description: This is as simple as it gets! You want to get data from a table? Just write the table name.

join.title: Join
join.description: Join tables without having to think of the foreign key relationships. Simply pipe tables together to create joins. However, if you want to specify the join column or other aspects of the join, you can pass the relevant arguments. See examples below:

examples.title: Join
examples.description: Two tables based using the foreign key.

examples.title: Multi-table join
examples.description: Pipe multiple tables together for joining multiple tables

examples.title: Schema qualified join
examples.description: Use schema qualification when joining across different schemas

examples.title: Left join
examples.description: Use the :left modifier to specify a left join

examples.title: Self join
examples.description: Join a table with itself

examples.title: Self join with direction / Parent-child relationship
examples.description: By default, the child table is picked for the join i.e. the one that holds the foreing key. If you want to join on the parent table i.e. the one being referenced, then use the :parent modifier. Aliases are used for demonstration purposes.

examples.title: Join on values in a JSON array
examples.description: [*] means any element of the array. Each project joins to every employee whose id is in its members array. The new table's column comes first. A row joins once per match. Values compare as JSON, so the number 5 doesn't match the string "5".

examples.title: Join on a name you give
examples.description: A name given with as tells Pine what a column holds. company_id leads to the companies table, by the same rule Pine uses for column names. Use it when no foreign key says it, as here: resource_id holds the ids of several tables, and only the where: makes sure they are company ids.

examples.title: Name the table on each side
examples.description: Each side of a pair can name its table's alias, so one join can compare with any table before it. Here addresses joins to customers and to orders. A side without an alias keeps its usual meaning: written first, the table being joined; written second, the table just before it.

examples.title: Conditions on the join
examples.description: A pair can compare a column with a value, or test is null. The condition stays on the join. On a :left join that keeps every customer and attaches only their paid orders. The same test in where: would drop the customers without one.

modifiers: <1>:left</1> - Performs a left outer join, keeping all records from the left table
<1>:right</1> - Performs a right outer join, keeping all records from the right table
<1>:parent</1> - Joins on the parent table (the one being referenced) instead of the child table (the one with the foreign key)

paths.title: Paths
paths.description: Ask Pine how two tables connect, and it searches for every join chain between them - not just the direct next hop. Useful the moment you know you need data from another table but not how to get there.

examples.title: Direct and multi-hop
examples.description: Returns every route from company to document, not just the next hop. If employee sits in between (company → employee → document) as well as a direct company_id column on document, both come back - ordered so the genuine relationship ranks above the denormalized shortcut.

examples.title: Composed on top of an existing expression
examples.description: The search starts from wherever the pipe left off, not from a bare table name - everything before the ? is an ordinary, fully composable Pine expression.

paths.intro1: A single pipe (<1>customers | orders</1>) already shows what a table can join to next. <3>?</3> answers a different question: how would you even get from one table to another, when the real connection is two or three hops away through a table you hadn't thought to name.
paths.intro2: Each result is a real Pine expression, ready to drop in place of the <1>? table</1> segment - not a query result. A few things to know:
notes: Routes are ranked by how meaningful the connection is, not by hop count alone - a shortcut column that only duplicates a longer, more direct relationship ranks behind the real one, even when it's shorter.
<1>?</1> is terminal - nothing meaningful follows it in the same pipe, the same as <3>count:</3> or bare <5>delete:</5>.
It has no table modifiers of its own (no <1>as alias</1>, no <3>.hint_column</3>, no <5>:parent</5>) - the named table is a search destination, not something being joined directly.
Results are capped so a densely-connected schema can't turn a lookup into a long-running search.

describe.title: Describe
describe.description: See a table's columns, as a result you can read. describe: reads the schema Beamlynx already knows, so nothing runs on your database.

examples.title: A table's columns
examples.description: One row per column, with its type, and whether it is the key, may be empty or is masked.

examples.title: After a join
examples.description: describe: describes the table the pipe left off at: here, employee.

describe.intro1: Each row has five columns: <1>column</1>, <3>type</3>, <5>key</5> (primary for a column of the primary key), <7>nullable</7> (yes when it may be empty) and <9>masked</9> (yes when the masking policy masks it).
notes: A masked column's name still shows: masking hides values, not names.
describe: ends a query for now. Nothing can follow it. To see how a table connects to others, use references:.
In the app, a table's <1>+</1> menu on the canvas has <3>describe</3>, which opens it in a new tab.

references.title: References
references.description: See every relation that touches a table, both ways: the keys it holds of other tables, and the keys other tables hold of it. references: reads the schema Beamlynx already knows, so nothing runs on your database.

examples.title: The tables that refer to one
examples.description: One row per relation: which side holds the key, which it points at, how Beamlynx knows it, and the Pine to follow it.

examples.title: A table that holds keys
examples.description: employee holds a key of company, so that relation shows too, with the Pine to go from employee to company.

references.intro1: Each row has four columns: <1>from</1> (the side holding the key), <3>to</3> (the side it points at), <5>how</5> and <7>pine</7> (what to type after a pipe to follow it).
notes: how says foreign key when the database declares the relation, and naming when Beamlynx infers it from a column's name, such as company_id.
A table that refers to itself, such as employee.reports_to, shows twice: once each way.
references: ends a query for now. Nothing can follow it.
In the app, a table's <1>+</1> menu on the canvas has <3>references</3>, which opens it in a new tab.

where.title: Where
where.description: Filters the results based on conditions. Inside one where:, join conditions with or. To require several conditions, add a where: step for each.

examples.title: Condition
examples.description: Filter records where a column equals a specific value

examples.title: Every condition
examples.description: Chain where: steps to keep only rows that match all of them

examples.title: NULL
examples.description: Filter for records with NULL values in a column

examples.title: NOT NULL
examples.description: Filter for records with NOT NULL values in a column

examples.title: IN clause
examples.description: Filter for records where column value matches any in a list

examples.title: Column comparison
examples.description: Compare values between different columns

examples.title: LIKE
examples.description: Filter for records using the LIKE operator

examples.title: ILIKE
examples.description: Filter for records using the ILIKE operator

examples.title: Either condition
examples.description: Join conditions with or to keep rows that match any of them

examples.title: A function of a column
examples.description: A condition can start with a function of a column, compared with a value. data => jsonb_typeof = 'array' means the same.

json.title: JSON
json.description: Use a key inside a json or jsonb column wherever a column goes: write the column, then each key after a dot. It works in select:, where:, order:, group: and update!, on PostgreSQL and MySQL. Keys are sent as parameters, never pasted into the SQL.

examples.title: Pick out a value
examples.description: Each key follows a dot. The result column is named after the path, unless 'as' names it.

examples.title: Filter on a value
examples.description: The value decides how it compares: 10 as a number, 'SE' as text. '>' and '<' only match values of the same kind, so a row whose seats is the text '20' or a boolean is skipped.

examples.title: Missing keys
examples.description: 'is null' matches a row without the key, and a row where the key is null.

examples.title: Group by a key
examples.description: Count rows per value of a key, like any column.

examples.title: Arrays and unusual keys
examples.description: [0] is the first element of an array. A key with spaces or other characters is quoted.

examples.title: Through an alias
examples.description: A name before the first dot is an alias when one exists, otherwise a column of the current table. If both exist, the alias wins.

examples.title: Change one value
examples.description: update! replaces the value at a key and leaves the rest of the JSON as it was. The value keeps the kind you write: 12 is a number, '12' is text. Editing such a cell in the results does the same.

examples.title: The type of a value
examples.description: jsonb_typeof gives object, array, string, number, boolean or null, with the same names on every database. A missing key gives no value.

examples.title: Count an array's items
examples.description: jsonb_array_length counts the items in an array. On PostgreSQL, a value that isn't an array is an error; MySQL and SQLite give no value. x => f means the same as f(x).

examples.title: An array, or an array inside
examples.description: Check the type first when a value may not be an array. Inside these two functions a key is read as JSON, and so is each branch of an if. Elsewhere a key is text, so an if that gives the whole column in one branch and a key in another fails on PostgreSQL.

examples.title: One row per element
examples.description: unnest: gives one row for each element of an array, next to the row it came from. Read the element's keys through the name after as. A row whose value isn't an array is skipped. This works on PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite.

examples.title: Keep rows without an array
examples.description: :left keeps a row whose value isn't an array once, with the element empty. For an array of strings or numbers, the name on its own is the element.

select.title: Select
select.description: Select columns to return in the query result.

examples.title: Select specific columns
examples.description: Choose only the columns you need in the result

examples.title: Select with alias
examples.description: Rename columns in the output using aliases

examples.title: Select with table qualification
examples.description: Specify which table each column comes from in joins

computedValues.title: Computed values
computedValues.description: A value that isn't just a column: a fallback, a flag, a label, a date cut to its month. In select:, give it a name with as. Later steps use the name like a column. The functions are coalesce, concat, now and the date units minute, hour, day, week, month and year. In group:, the aggregates are count, min, max, sum, avg, any and all.

examples.title: A fallback
examples.description: coalesce gives the first value that isn't empty. concat joins values as text, and is empty when any part is.

examples.title: A flag
examples.description: A condition in select: is a true or false column.

examples.title: A label chosen by a condition
examples.description: if ... then ... else picks a value. Chain branches with else if. Without else, the value is empty when no condition holds.

examples.title: The arrow
examples.description: x => f is f(x), so a value grows by adding steps at the end. month, year, day, week, hour and minute cut a date to that unit.

examples.title: Use the name later
examples.description: A later where:, order:, group: or limit: per uses the name like a column. Pine writes the value out again there, since SQL can't use a SELECT name in WHERE.

examples.title: Totals per group
examples.description: In group:, the keys come first, then with and the aggregates.

order.title: Order
order.description: Sort the results by one or more columns.

examples.title: Basic ordering
examples.description: Sort results by a single column in ascending order

examples.title: Descending order
examples.description: Sort results in descending order using the desc keyword. Descending is also the default when you write neither asc nor desc.

examples.title: Multiple columns
examples.description: Sort by multiple columns with different sort directions

examples.title: Empty values first
examples.description: nulls first puts the rows with no value first, and nulls last puts them last. Without it, each database decides: PostgreSQL puts them last when sorting ascending, MySQL and SQLite put them first.

limit.title: Limit
limit.description: The limit operation restricts the number of rows returned from a query. Use 'limit:' or the shorthand 'l:' to specify the maximum number of rows.

examples.title: Limit
examples.description: Get the first 10 rows from the customers table

examples.title: Limit with filter
examples.description: Filter customers and limit to 5 results

examples.title: Limit after join
examples.description: Join customers and orders, filter by total amount, then limit results

from.title: From
from.description: The from operation sets the context for subsequent operations in complex queries. Use 'from:' or the shorthand 'f:' to specify which table or alias to use as the source for the next operations.

examples.title: Context switch with status tracking
examples.description: Get order status history by joining order items and status changes, using from to maintain order context

group.title: Group
group.description: Used to group the results of a query by a given column.

examples.title: Basic grouping
examples.description: Group products by category and count the number of order items for each category

count.title: Count
count.description: The count operation returns the total number of rows in a result set. Use 'count:' to get the row count of your query results.

examples.title: Simple Count
examples.description: Count all rows in the categories table

delete.title: Delete
delete.description: The delete operation removes rows from a table. All side-effect operations in pine-lang are suffixed with '!' to indicate they modify data. Use delete! to permanently remove records that match your filter conditions.

examples.title: Delete Specific Record
examples.description: Delete the customer with the email 'john.doe@email.com' from the customers table

variables.title: Variables
variables.description: Name an intermediate result and use it as a table in later expressions. Variables let you build up queries in readable steps instead of nesting subqueries.

examples.title: Name a result and reuse it
examples.description: Assign the filtered company result to active_companies, then use it as a table in the next expression.

examples.title: Mid-pipeline assign
examples.description: Place |= anywhere in the pipe chain. The snapshot is taken at that point — all_companies is the full unfiltered company set, while the current expression still returns only active companies.

examples.title: Reference variable columns
examples.description: After |= c, use c as a column qualifier in the same expression. c.id refers to the company table's id column.

examples.title: Chain multiple steps
examples.description: Each expression builds on the previous. Separate expressions with a blank line.

examples.title: Only explicitly selected id columns stay joinable
examples.description: Once a variable is used, its underlying tables are no longer visible — only its own output columns are. A table stays a valid join source through the variable only if its id was explicitly selected. select: name alone (no id) would make x unjoinable to anything.

examples.title: Automatic checkpoints after group: or limit:
examples.description: group: and limit: produce a final, bounded result. Piping into another table after one of them automatically wraps the preceding query in an anonymous CTE first, so the join applies on top of the limited/grouped result instead of corrupting it. Name that CTE yourself with |= placed right after the group:/limit: step.

examples.title: Combine multiple aggregates per row
examples.description: x and y each aggregate a different related table down to one row per customer, exposing just their own count column. The final expression starts from customers again and joins both variables in, producing one row per customer with email, order_count, and status_change_count side by side — without nesting subqueries or repeating the customers join in each branch.

agents.title: AI agents
agents.description: Beamlynx can let an AI agent, such as Claude Code, query the databases you choose. The agent works in Pine, and every query it runs shows in the Beamlynx app, where you can follow it.
intro: The desktop app runs an MCP server: the standard way an AI agent talks to a tool on your computer. The agent asks Beamlynx about your tables, builds a query one step at a time, and runs it. Each query opens in a tab in the app, next to a timeline of what the agent has done.

Agents write Pine. They can also send SQL with <1>run_sql_as_pine</1>: Beamlynx converts it to Pine, and only the Pine runs. SQL that Pine can't express runs nothing, and the agent is told why. An agent never changes your data. Only you can run an update or a delete.

setup.title: Connect an agent
steps: In Beamlynx, click <1>Agent</1> in the sidebar and open the <3>Setup</3> tab.
Copy what it shows for your agent. It holds the path to Beamlynx on your computer.
setup.claudeCode: For Claude Code, run the command in a terminal. It looks like this:
setup.otherClients: For other MCP clients, paste the configuration into the client's MCP settings, such as Claude Desktop's <1>claude_desktop_config.json</1>:
setup.databases: Then choose which databases the agent may use, on the <1>Databases</1> tab. A database is off until you turn it on, and turning it on masks it with the recommended rules.

tools.title: What the agent can do
tools.intro: The agent gets these tools. Each is a way to reach what Pine and the app already do; none of them can do more than you can in the app.

items.list_connections: Lists the databases you turned on for agents. Any other database doesn't exist as far as the agent can tell.
items.find_tables: Finds tables by part of their name, the same way the app suggests a table when you start typing. "ten" finds <1>tenant</1>.
items.complete_query: Says what can come next in a Pine expression: the tables it can join to, or a table's columns. It is how the agent builds a query step by step instead of guessing. It runs nothing.
items.run_query: Runs a Pine expression and returns the rows. The query opens in a tab in the app, so you see what ran. Without a limit of its own, a result stops at 250 rows and says so. The agent can send what it is investigating and what it has found with the query: the question titles its timeline, and a new question starts a new section.
items.run_sql_as_pine: Takes SQL, converts it to Pine and runs the Pine, the same as run_query, question and findings included. The answer starts with the Pine, so the agent learns how to write it.
items.get_pine_doc: Reads one topic of the Pine reference, with examples.
items.set_question: Names what the agent is investigating. Being replaced by the question sent with run_query, and still works for now.
items.note_finding: Records something the agent found. Being replaced by the finding sent with run_query, and still works for now.
items.get_access_policy: Reads which columns the agent may see on a database: the masking rules, never data.
items.propose_policy_change: Asks you to change the masking rules. Nothing changes until you click Apply in the app.
items.open_in_desktop: Gives you a link that opens a Pine expression in the app, for you to look at yourself.

tools.describe: To learn a table, the agent runs two Pine operations with run_query, the same ones you can run in the app. <1>describe:</1> lists the table's columns: each one's type and key, whether it may be empty, and whether it is masked. <1>references:</1> lists how the table joins to other tables, both ways, with what to type for each join.

masking.title: Data masking
masking.0: Each database an agent can use has masking rules. A masked column's values come back to the agent as "xxxxx". The agent can still filter, sort and join on a masked column, because the value it compares with is its own. It just never sees the values.
masking.1: You set the rules on the Agent page, under Masking. The recommended rules show numbers, ids, dates, true/false values and keys, and mask everything else, such as text and JSON. Text is where names, emails and notes usually are.

proposals.title: Change proposals
proposals.0: When an agent needs to see a masked column, it proposes a change to the masking rules, such as showing that one column, with its reason. The proposal waits in the agent's timeline until you apply or decline it. Nothing changes without you.
